title: Release-free phononic crystal with strong microwave coupling
authors: Joey Frey, Paul Burger, Trond Hjerpekjøn Haug, Johan Kolvik, Raphaël Van Laer
abstract: Phonons hold promise for storing and transferring quantum information, including in mechanically-mediated quantum interconnects between superconducting qubits and light. Phononic crystal cavities confine gigahertz sound to micron-scale volumes well matched to near-infrared light. So far, these devices have typically been suspended to suppress phononic radiation loss into the substrate, but suspension limits thermal anchoring leading to excess noise. Release-free phononic crystals have emerged as a way to address this challenge -- but had yet to be shown compatible with strong electromechanical interactions. Here, we demonstrate a release-free phononic crystal cavity strongly coupled to a high-impedance microwave resonator, with an electromechanical coupling rate $g_\mathrm{em}/(2π) \approx 30\,\text{MHz}$ that exceeds both the mechanical and microwave loss rates, leading to a cooperativity up to $\mathcal{C} \approx 180$ on resonance. In addition, our lithium niobate phononic crystals reach quality factors above $10^4$ at millikelvin temperature on both silicon and sapphire substrates. Our results establish release-free phononic crystals as compact, scalable interfaces between microwaves and gigahertz sound for emerging sensing, communication, and computing systems.
summary: The paper reports on the realization of a release-free phononic crystal cavity that strongly couples microwave photons to gigahertz acoustic phonons. By overcoming the noise limitations of suspended structures, they demonstrate high cooperativity and excellent quality factors, establishing this platform as a scalable interface for quantum information processing.
main_problem: The challenge is creating compact, scalable interfaces between microwaves and gigahertz sound (phonons) for quantum applications while avoiding the noise issues associated with suspended phononic structures.
main_result: The authors demonstrated a release-free phononic crystal cavity strongly coupled to a microwave resonator, achieving strong coupling parameters ($\mathcal{C} \approx 180$) and high quality factors ($Q > 10^4$).
method: Experimental characterization using microwave reflection/transmission spectroscopy at cryogenic temperatures (down to 10 mK) combined with finite-element method simulations.
model_or_system: The system utilizes release-free phononic crystal cavities patterned in lithium niobate ($	ext{LiNbO}_3$) on silicon or sapphire, coupled electromechanically via an Interdigital Transducer (IDT) to a high-impedance microwave resonator.
key_observables: Electromechanical coupling rate ($g_{em}/(2\pi)$), Cooperativity ($\mathcal{C}$), internal mechanical quality factor ($Q_i$), and microwave reflection/transmission spectra ($S_{11}, S_{21}$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the release-free structure can maintain strong coupling comparable to suspended devices while offering better thermal anchoring and scalability.
figures_summary: Figures show device schematics, mechanical band diagrams, mode simulations, SEM images of fabricated devices, and cryogenic measurement setups used for characterizing coupling strength and quality factors.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the need for robust phononic interfaces to demonstrating strong coupling in a release-free geometry, quantifying performance metrics like cooperativity and $Q$ factor across different temperature regimes.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses quantum transduction—the critical link needed to connect superconducting qubits (microwave domain) to mechanical oscillators (phonon domain)—which is central to quantum networking architectures.
